title: Fireworks
mood: Eleven cakes, a teacup that spins, a box nobody knows about, and a curfew broken for the summer fireworks.

hero.alt: Comic panel at night: two girls in school uniform, seen from behind, hold hands under bursting fireworks; the one with red bows and a red skirt points at the sky, and the long dark-haired girl beside her watches her face instead.
hero.credit: Official Guinevere and Vexana comic, page 22

segs.t: Vexana stood in front of the menu board and read it for the third time.

The girls’ house was a cake shop halfway down the hill from the Academy, under a pink awning. Only girls went in. Half the girls at the Academy came here on rest days, and all of them knew what to order.
At the home, food had come on a tray when the bell rang. Nobody had ever asked her what she wanted.
She had left the toolbox in her room today. Her shoulder felt wrong without it.
“Take your time,” said Guinevere. She turned to the counter. “One of everything on the top row.”
“That’s eleven cakes,” said the girl behind it.
“Then eleven.”
“You’ve been here before,” said Vexana.
“Never,” said Guinevere. “Everyone else has.”
She had the black card halfway out. She stopped, and looked at Vexana.
“My treat,” she said. “You get the next one.”
It was a question. Vexana heard that it was.
“The next one,” said Vexana.
The cakes came on two trays. When the teapot was empty, Vexana went up to the counter herself. She paid for a second pot out of the band she had broken for the felt.
The felt was for Guinevere,
she thought.
This is for me.
Over the table hung the drone she had mended on the grass. It held its height now.
Guinevere held a strawberry-jam doughnut up to it. The drone circled the doughnut twice. Guinevere grinned.
“Nothing can resist a strawberry-jam doughnut. Even robots are the same.”
She tore the doughnut in two and held out half in its paper napkin. Vexana ate it. Jam got on her glove.
When Guinevere turned to the window, Vexana folded the napkin into a small square and put it in her pocket.
Eight cakes were left. They went into a white box tied with string.
Outside on the step a woman in a gray coat was waiting. Vexana had seen that coat before, at the wheel of a long car at the Academy gate.
“That’s Hester,” said Guinevere. “Ignore her.” She put the box in Hester’s hands. “There’s one in there for you.”
“Yes, miss,” said Hester.
All afternoon at the amusement park, Hester walked two steps behind them with the box.

Guinevere bought a strip of ride tickets at the gate. At every ride the attendant tore a ticket in half and handed back the stub. Guinevere put each one in Vexana’s hand without looking. Vexana put each one in her pocket with the napkin.
On the teacup ride, Hester sat in the next cup. She spun with them, upright, the white box on her knees, with no expression at all.
Something tugged at the corner of Vexana’s mouth. She pressed it flat.
Every time their cup swung past, Guinevere waved at Hester. Hester never waved back. Guinevere waved anyway, and laughed.
Everyone who ever stayed near her,
thought Vexana,
was paid to stay.
By the third ride Vexana’s black hair was hot to the touch. Guinevere bought a paper fan painted with goldfish from a cart and fanned her hard. Then she pushed it into Vexana’s hand.
“Keep it. You’re cooking.”
Near the way out, a stall sold keychains: tiny dolls with big heads, one for every color of hair.
Guinevere took a black-haired one and a pink-haired one. She hung the black-haired keychain on her own belt. Then she pressed the pink one into Vexana’s palm.
“Now you have me on yours.”
The old words came up in Vexana.
I cannot repay...
She clipped the keychain to her belt instead.
At the Academy gate, Hester handed back the box. It was one cake lighter.
Guinevere put it in Vexana’s arms. “Midnight snack. That’s an order.”
That night Vexana ate one cake at her desk, as ordered. The rest went onto a plate. She wiped the white box clean inside.
Into it went the ticket stubs, the paper fan, the napkin from the doughnut, folded small, jam and all.
She looked at them for a long time.
Stubs. A fan. A napkin,
she thought.
Nobody could call those debts.
She unclipped the pink keychain from her belt and laid it in with them. She unpinned her star and laid it beside the keychain.
In the morning the star went back on her collar and the keychain on her belt. At night they went back in the box. It became the last thing she did each day.
She never told Guinevere about the box.

Before she slept that night, she took the brown paper out of her drawer and unfolded the felt. At the home the children mended their own clothes. She threaded a needle. From the pink she cut a small round head, then another from the black.
Her first stitches came out too tight. She picked them out, and began again.
The night of the summer fireworks.

Every summer of her childhood, Guinevere had watched the fireworks from the House’s terrace on the hill. From up there they were no bigger than her thumbnail. A guard stood at each end of the terrace.
At the Academy, they started after the curfew bell. After curfew, nobody went out of the grounds.
Vexana kept every rule. In all their weeks as partners, Guinevere had never once seen her break one. She had never seen her do anything just because she wanted to, either.
She knocked on Vexana’s door anyway.
Vexana opened it, stepped out and shut it behind her. She always did. Guinevere had never seen past that door.
“The fireworks,” said Guinevere. “Out at the dome’s edge. Let’s go.”
“It’s after curfew.”
“I know.”
“We’ll be caught.”
“Rules are for keeping safe what matters,” said Guinevere. “Not for locking you up.”
Vexana looked at her and did not move.
Guinevere took her hand. “Until dawn arrives, I will never let go of your hand.”
“Dawn is seven hours away,” said Vexana.
“Then seven hours.”
Night lamps burned along one wall of the corridor. Guinevere went down it under the lamps, pulling. Vexana came along the dark side, her hand in Guinevere’s.
Halfway to the stairs, the pull went out of Guinevere’s arm. Vexana was keeping up.
The kitchen yard had a gate in its wall, bolted on the inside and nothing more. At the House the guards had always found her. Here nobody was paid to look for her. She slid the bolt.
Out in the street she looked back. Nobody walked two steps behind them.
She laughed out loud, and ran.
Vexana stopped where the last houses ended. She was out of breath, and Guinevere’s hand was still tight in hers.
Seven hours,
she thought.
The shelter door came back to her. She had slipped out under a stranger’s arm, because she only wanted to be with her father.
She listened for the guns. She heard the wind, and Guinevere getting her breath back.
Past the houses the ground ran on, open and dark, to the dome’s edge. The crowds were down at the bay front. Out here there was only grass, and the two of them in their school uniforms.
The first rocket went up with a thin whistle. Vexana’s hand closed hard on Guinevere’s.
Pink broke open overhead, then gold. The bursts came one after another, and their light ran over the grass and back.
Guinevere pointed at the sky. Vexana watched her face instead. Every burst lit it a new color.
“We’ll be just like fireworks, shining at our absolute brightest!” said Guinevere.
At their collars, both stars glowed faintly.
Don’t get used to this,
Vexana told herself.
You’ll only have to give it back.
Between two bursts the smoke drifted clear. Far above the dome, a thin line of light slid down the dark and was gone.
“A shooting star!” Guinevere squeezed her hand. “Quick, make a wish!” She shut her eyes tight. Her lips moved.
Vexana missed the star. She was watching Guinevere, eyes screwed shut, wishing hard for something with her whole face.
Just for this moment,
thought Vexana.
Let time stop.
The corner of her mouth lifted again. This time she did not press it flat. She was smiling.
Her star went warm, then bright.
Guinevere opened her eyes. The star at her collar flared to match. She did not look back at the sky.
Guinevere’s voice came out soft. “It’s not only shooting stars that shine. Vexana, your smile does too.”
Vexana did not answer. She did not let go.
Overhead the next burst opened, pink and gold. It showed again, small, in the two stars at their collars.
Both were lit.
